newsitem.title: USA: WHO says new vaccines in works -- but at a price.
newsitem.headline: WHO says new vaccines in works -- but at a price.

text.p: Scientists are developing vaccines that could save the lives of millions of children a year, but the price may prove a huge barrier to poor nations, world health officials said on Wednesday.

A report by the World Health Organisation (WHO) and UNICEF surveyed progress in reaching children around the world with vaccines now available and prospects for new or improved vaccines that could save up to 8 million more children a year within 10 or 15 years.

"The 21st century is the century of the vaccine," said Dr. Ciro de Quadros, a top WHO adviser on immunisation. But he added, "The vaccine of the future will be more expensive than the vaccine of today."

Many of the newer vaccines use genetic or molecular biology technology that is much more expensive than the older vaccines that cost a few cents a dose. Vaccine development also occurs mainly in the private sector in industrialised countries and these vaccines may not work as well against the slightly different strains of diseases in poorer countries, where the market is not as profitable for drug companies.

Scientists and health officials at a WHO briefing in Washington also pointed out that vaccines were a potent weapon against diseases and infections that were becoming dangerously resistant to antibiotics.

WHO and UNICEF noted huge successes in the past two decades. Since 1974, the percentage of children vaccinated against polio, measles, tetanus, diphtheria, whooping cough and tuberculosis has risen from 5 percent to 80 percent of the 130 million children born each year.

That drive against those six childhood killers, carried out under the Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI), saves an estimated two million more lives a year. But of the 12 million children under age 5 who die each year, 2 million die from diseases that could be prevented by vaccines. In some African nations, vaccination rates are still only about 50 percent.

Vaccines against hepatitis B and yellow fever have been added to the EPI list but are not yet widely available in developing nations. For instance, of 33 countries identified as at risk for yellow fever, vaccine coverage was only 9 percent in 1994. In some places, it was all but nonexistent.

In recent years there has been a shift so that all but the poorest countries have become self-sufficient in paying for EPI vaccines, which cost only a few pennies each. But the next generation of vaccines, against diseases like rotavirus, shigella, dengue and meningitis, may cost dollars instead.
WHO and UNICEF outlined four major goals to get around what they called a "herculean" funding task.

They are not asking for free vaccines for poor countries but they do want more "tiered pricing" so that manufacturers charge less to poorer nations. They also want governments and donors to commit to spend more on vaccines and they want aid targeted better to countries in most need.
They also said more public health and advocacy was required so that governments and donor countries, which may not balk at expensive drugs and hospital expenses, recognise the value of vaccines.

"In the long run, treatment to save the lives of children not immunised against vaccine-preventable diseases and the legacy of disabled children will cost a lot more -- both in money and needless suffering for children and their families," the agencies concluded.
